title: "4.3 Pydantic schemas: requests, responses, PATCH vs PUT"
description: "Describe what clients may send and what they get back with Pydantic models, keep secrets out of responses, and update resources correctly with PATCH and PUT."
---

::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 4 · Lesson 3 · About 75 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: forms at a bank counter"}
To open an account you fill in a form with fixed boxes: name, address, a signature of a certain kind. The clerk rejects a form with an empty box or a date in the wrong format before doing anything. When you ask for a statement, you get a different, printed form: your balance and transactions, never the bank's internal notes or your PIN.

A **schema** is one of those forms. The *request* schema says what a client may send; the *response* schema says exactly what goes back. They are separate forms on purpose.
:::

## Theory

A **schema** is a description of the shape of some data: which fields, of which types, with which rules. In FastAPI you write schemas as **Pydantic models**: classes that inherit from `BaseModel`, with one type-hinted attribute per field.

When a route has a parameter whose type is a Pydantic model, FastAPI reads the **JSON request body** into it. If the body doesn't match, the client gets 422 and your function never runs. When a route has a **response model**, FastAPI filters and converts whatever the function returns into that shape.

### Models versus schemas

Atlas already has *models* (`models.py`, lesson 3.8): classes mapped to database tables. Schemas describe the HTTP boundary. They differ deliberately:

| | `User` model (table) | `UserOut` schema (response) |
|---|---|---|
| `password_hash` | yes | **no** |
| `email` | yes | yes |
| purpose | storage | what clients may see |

If a route returned the table object directly, every column, including `password_hash`, would leak. The response model is a whitelist.

### Validation rules

`Field(...)` adds rules to a field: `min_length`, `max_length`, `ge` (greater or equal), `le`, `pattern` (a regular expression, lesson 1.7). Special types validate formats: `EmailStr` checks an email address. `Literal["user", "admin"]` allows only those exact values.

### PUT versus PATCH

Both change an existing resource, but they mean different things in HTTP (lesson 2.3):

- **PUT** replaces the resource with what you send. Fields you leave out are reset. Sending the same PUT twice gives the same result: PUT is **idempotent**.
- **PATCH** changes only the fields you send. Everything else stays.

For PATCH, every field in the schema is optional, and the route must tell "not sent" apart from "sent as null". Pydantic remembers which fields were actually set: `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` returns only those.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  B["JSON body"] -->|validate| I[UserCreate<br/>email, password]
  I --> R[route function]
  R -->|"User (ORM object)"| O[UserOut<br/>whitelist]
  O -->|JSON without password_hash| C[client]
```

## In the project

`src/atlas/api/schemas.py` holds every request and response shape. The user schemas:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, EmailStr, Field


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    password: str = Field(min_length=10, max_length=128)


class UserOut(BaseModel):
    # from_attributes lets Pydantic read user.email from an ORM object, not only dict keys.
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

    id: int
    email: EmailStr | None
    github_login: str | None
    role: Literal["user", "admin"]
    skills_profile: str
    created_at: datetime


class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    """PATCH body: every field optional, so a client can change just one."""

    skills_profile: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000)
```

`EmailStr` needs the `email-validator` package: `uv add email-validator`. Why a maximum password length? Hashing (lesson 4.7) is deliberately slow; a megabyte-long "password" would make every login attempt expensive for the server.

Using them in routes (lesson 4.7 fills in the bodies):

```python
@router.post("/register", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED, response_model=UserOut)
def register(body: UserCreate, session: SessionDep) -> User:
    ...


@router.patch("/me", response_model=UserOut)
def update_me(changes: UserUpdate, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> User:
    # exclude_unset: only the fields the client actually sent, so PATCH changes just those.
    for field, value in changes.model_dump(exclude_unset=True).items():
        setattr(user, field, value)
    session.commit()
    session.refresh(user)
    return user
```

The function returns a `User` table object; `response_model=UserOut` turns it into the safe shape. `status_code=201` is HTTP's "Created". `setattr(user, field, value)` sets the attribute named by the string `field`, so the loop works for any field the schema adds later.

Real output once lessons 4.7 and 4.8 are done:

```text
$ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email": "ada@example.com", "password": "correct-horse-battery"}'
{"id":3,"email":"ada@example.com","github_login":null,"role":"user","skills_profile":"","created_at":"2026-11-18T03:10:48.623999Z"}

$ curl -s -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/users/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"skills_profile\": \"metrics, handlers\"}"
{"id":3,"email":"ada@example.com","github_login":null,"role":"user","skills_profile":"metrics, handlers","created_at":"2026-11-18T03:10:48.623999Z"}
```

No password or hash in the response, and the PATCH changed only `skills_profile`. A body that breaks the rules never reaches the function:

```text
$ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email": "not-an-email", "password": "short"}'
{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"The request is not valid","request_id":"bc087dbefa5b4a35a92873271d9edac0","details":[{"location":["body","email"],"message":"value is not a valid email address: An email address must have an @-sign."},{"location":["body","password"],"message":"String should have at least 10 characters"}]}}
```

(The `{"error": ...}` shape is Atlas's own, from lesson 4.14.)

The rest of `schemas.py` follows the same pattern: `RepoCreate` (with `pattern=r"^[\w.-]+/[\w.-]+$"` so only `owner/name` is accepted), `IssueOut`, `SearchHit`, and page wrappers used in lesson 4.12.

## Common mistakes

- **Returning table objects without a response model**: every column leaks, including hashes and internal flags.
- **One schema for input and output**: then `id` and `created_at` look like things a client may send, and `password` looks like something you return.
- **PATCH with `model_dump()` instead of `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)`**: unsent fields come through as `None` and wipe stored values.
- **Validating by hand inside the route** (`if len(password) < 10: ...`). Put rules in the schema: they run before your code, and they appear in the docs.
- **Forgetting `from_attributes=True`** when a response model is built from an ORM object: Pydantic then expects a dict.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why does Atlas have both a `User` model and a `UserOut` schema?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The model describes the table, including `password_hash`. The schema describes what clients may see. Keeping them separate means a new secret column can never appear in a response by accident; the schema is a whitelist.
:::

**2.** A client sends `PATCH /users/me` with `{}`. What changes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Nothing. `exclude_unset=True` returns an empty dict, so the loop sets no attributes. With a plain `model_dump()`, `skills_profile` would be set to `None`.
:::

**3.** Is `POST /auth/register` idempotent? Is `PUT`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
POST isn't: a second identical request tries to create a second account (Atlas answers 409). PUT is: replacing a resource with the same content twice leaves it the same. Lesson 4.16 shows how to make POSTs safe to retry with idempotency keys.
:::

## Exercise

Add an optional `display_name` to `UserUpdate` (1 to 50 characters). Without changing the model, what does `UserUpdate(display_name="")` raise? And what does `UserUpdate().model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` return?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
display_name: str | None = Field(default=None, min_length=1, max_length=50)
```
`UserUpdate(display_name="")` raises a `ValidationError`: "String should have at least 1 character". `UserUpdate().model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` returns `{}`. (To store it you'd also add a column and a migration, lesson 4.13.)
:::

## Stretch

Write a test proving `UserOut` can't leak the hash: build a `User(email="a@b.c", password_hash="$argon2...", ...)` object in memory, validate it with `UserOut.model_validate(user)` and assert `"password_hash"` isn't in `model_dump()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from atlas.api.schemas import UserOut
from atlas.models import User


def test_user_out_has_no_hash() -> None:
    user = User(id=1, email="a@b.c", password_hash="$argon2id$fake", role="user",
                skills_profile="", created_at=datetime.now(UTC))

    dumped = UserOut.model_validate(user).model_dump()

    assert "password_hash" not in dumped
```
No database is needed: the object is never added to a session.
:::
